section.title: The Decision Problem of a Theory
section.para: A theory T is a set of sentences closed under logical consequence in some fixed logical framework. The decision problem of T asks whether there exists a finite, effective method that, given any sentence φ in the language of T, determines in finitely many steps whether φ is or is not a theorem of T.

A theory T is called decidable if there exists a method by means of which, for every sentence φ formulated in the terms of T, it can be decided in a finite number of steps whether φ is or is not provable (i.e., derivable) in T; otherwise T is called undecidable.

blockquote.para: By a decision procedure for a given formalized theory T we understand a method which permits us to decide in each particular case whether a given sentence formulated in the symbolism of T can be proved by means of the devices available in T (or, more generally, can be recognized as valid in T).
The decision problem for T is the problem of determining whether a decision procedure for T exists (and possibly of exhibiting such a procedure).
A theory T is called decidable or undecidable according as the solution of the decision problem is positive or negative.
blockquote.attribution: Alfred Tarski, Andrzej Mostowski, and Raphael M. Robinson, Undecidable Theories, North-Holland, 1953, p. 3.
